PHP Syntax: PHP code is enclosed in <?php ... ?> tags. Statements end with semicolons. PHP can be embedded anywhere in HTML. Variables start with $. Whitespace is ignored. The closing ?> is optional at the end of a file (recommended to omit to prevent accidental output).

<?php
// This is a comment
echo "Hello World";

$name = "Alice";
$age = 30;
echo "$name is $age";

// No closing tag at end of pure PHP files
Data Types: PHP supports: string, int, float, bool, array, object, null, resource. Use var_dump() to inspect type and value. gettype() returns the type name. Type juggling happens automatically; use strict comparison (===, !==) to avoid surprises.

<?php
$s = "Hello";          // string
$i = 42;                // int
$f = 3.14;              // float
$b = true;              // bool
$a = [1, 2, 3];         // array
$n = null;              // null

var_dump($s, $i, $f, $b, $a, $n);

// Type juggling
var_dump('5' == 5);     // true (loose)
var_dump('5' === 5);    // false (strict)
Variables: PHP variables start with $ followed by a letter or underscore. They are dynamically typed and case-sensitive. Variables can be assigned by value or by reference (&). Variable variables ($$var) allow dynamic variable names.

<?php
$name = "Alice";
$age = 30;
$price = 19.99;
$is_active = true;

// By reference
$original = 10;
$ref = &$original;
$ref = 20;  // changes $original too

// Variable variables
$varName = "foo";
$$varName = "bar";  // $foo = "bar"
echo $foo;  // bar
What is PHP: PHP (Hypertext Preprocessor) is a widely-used open-source scripting language designed for web development. PHP code is executed on the server, generating HTML that is sent to the client. It can be embedded directly into HTML and works seamlessly with databases.
Constants & Magic Constants: define() defines runtime constants. const keyword defines compile-time constants (must be in top-level scope). Magic constants like __FILE__, __DIR__, __LINE__, __CLASS__, __METHOD__ change based on where they're used.

<?php
define('SITE_NAME', 'MyApp');
const VERSION = '1.0.0';

echo SITE_NAME;
echo VERSION;

// Magic constants
echo __FILE__;     // current file path
echo __DIR__;      // directory of current file
echo __LINE__;     // current line number
echo __CLASS__;    // current class name
Superglobals Deep: PHP superglobal arrays are automatically available in all scopes: $_GET, $_POST, $_REQUEST, $_SERVER, $_SESSION, $_COOKIE, $_FILES, $_ENV, $GLOBALS. $_SERVER provides request metadata: REQUEST_METHOD, HTTP_HOST, SERVER_NAME, REMOTE_ADDR, REQUEST_URI. Use filter_input() for safer access. Never trust raw superglobal values.

<?php
// $_SERVER details
var_dump($_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD']);  // GET, POST, etc.
var_dump($_SERVER['HTTP_HOST']);       // example.com
var_dump($_SERVER['REQUEST_URI']);     // /page?q=test
var_dump($_SERVER['REMOTE_ADDR']);     // client IP
var_dump($_SERVER['HTTP_USER_AGENT']);  // browser UA

// $_GET / $_POST
$search = $_GET['q'] ?? '';
$name = filter_input(INPUT_POST, 'name', FILTER_SANITIZE_STRING);

// $_ENV (from environment variables or .env)
$dbPass = $_ENV['DB_PASSWORD'] ?? '';

// $_FILES (file uploads)
// $_FILES['file']['name'], ['tmp_name'], ['size'], ['error']

// $GLOBALS — all variables in global scope
function debugGlobals(): void
{
    var_dump($GLOBALS['_SERVER']['REQUEST_METHOD']);
}

// $_REQUEST combines $_GET, $_POST, $_COOKIE (configurable)
// Avoid for security — explicit superglobal is safer
PHP Tags & Output: Multiple ways to output: echo (language construct), print (returns 1), printf (formatted), var_dump (debug info). Short echo tag <?= is shorthand for <?php echo. Always available in PHP 5.4+.

<?php
echo "Hello";
print "World";
printf("Value: %s", "test");

$arr = [1, 2, 3];
var_dump($arr);

// Short echo tag
?>
<?= "Hello from short tag" ?>
HTTP Headers & Status Codes: PHP controls HTTP responses via header() and http_response_code(). Set status codes: http_response_code(404). Set headers: header('Content-Type: application/json'). Redirect: header('Location: /login'); exit. Other headers: Cache-Control, Content-Disposition (file downloads), CORS headers. Headers must be sent before any output (or use output buffering).

<?php
// Set status code
http_response_code(201);  // Created

// Content type
header('Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8');

// Redirect
header('Location: /login');
// Always call exit after redirect header
exit;

// JSON response
echo json_encode(['status' => 'ok']);

// File download
header('Content-Type: application/pdf');
header('Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="report.pdf"');
header('Content-Length: ' . filesize('report.pdf'));
readfile('report.pdf');

// CORS headers
header('Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *');
header('Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE');
header('Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization');

// Cache control
header('Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate');
header('Pragma: no-cache');
header('Expires: 0');

// Previous header removal
header_remove('X-Powered-By');

Variables & Types.exp: Variables and data types in PHP.

Type Declarations & Coercion: PHP 7+ supports scalar type declarations (int, float, string, bool) for parameters and return types. By default, PHP coerces values (e.g., '5' becomes 5 for int). declare(strict_types=1) at file top enforces strict mode — no coercion, TypeError on mismatch. Strict mode is file-level, not project-level.

<?php
declare(strict_types=1);

function add(int $a, int $b): int {
    return $a + $b;
}

// Without strict_types: add('5', '3') works
// With strict_types: add('5', '3') = TypeError

// Void return
define_log(string $msg): void {
    error_log($msg);
}

// Never return (PHP 8.1+)
function abort(string $msg): never {
    throw new \RuntimeException($msg);
}

// Mixed type
function debug(mixed $value): void {
    var_dump($value);
}
Null & falsy Handling: PHP has isset() (checks if set and not null), empty() (falsey: '', 0, '0', null, false, []), is_null() (strict null check), and the null coalescing operator ?? (returns first non-null). Use ?? for defaults, ?-> for safe navigation (PHP 8+). The nullsafe operator stops chain on null.

<?php
$name = $_GET['name'] ?? 'Guest';

// isset vs empty
$var = 0;
var_dump(isset($var));  // true
var_dump(empty($var));  // true (0 is empty)

// Null coalescing chain
$city = $user?->address?->city ?? 'Unknown';

// Nullsafe operator (PHP 8+)
$length = $user?->getName()?->length();

// ??= (null coalescing assignment)
$cache ??= computeExpensiveValue();

// Null vs falsey
function getConfig(string $key): mixed {
    return $GLOBALS['config'][$key] ?? null;
}
Type Juggling Deep: PHP's type juggling converts types automatically in expressions. Loose comparison == coerces types; strict === checks type and value. Juggling rules: string to int (numeric prefix), bool to int (true=1, false=0), array to string ('Array'), object to bool (always true), null to string (''). Be careful with loose comparison of strings with numeric content.

<?php
// String to int
var_dump('5' + 3);      // int(8)
var_dump('5abc' + 3);   // int(8) — warns in PHP 8+
var_dump('abc' + 3);    // int(3) — warns in PHP 8+

// Loose vs strict
var_dump('1' == 1);     // true
var_dump('1' === 1);    // false
var_dump('' == false);  // true
var_dump('' === false); // false

// Tricky cases
var_dump(in_array('5abc', [5]));  // true (loose)
var_dump('0' == 0);     // true
var_dump('0' == false); // true

// PHP 8+ comparison improvements
// Floating point precision
var_dump(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3);  // false — use bccomp()
Constants (const vs define): Constants are immutable values. const is compile-time, must be at top level, and works in classes. define() is runtime, can be used anywhere. const can be used with expressions that are constant (1 + 2, __LINE__). define() accepts any expression. Use const when possible (faster, type-checked). Class constants are implicitly public, final.

<?php
// Global constants
const APP_NAME = 'MyApp';
define('APP_VERSION', '1.0.0');
define('DB_CONFIG', [
    'host' => 'localhost',
    'port' => 3306,
]);  // PHP 7+

// Class constants
class Database {
    const MYSQL = 'mysql';
    const PGSQL = 'pgsql';
    public const int MAX_RETRIES = 3;  // typed (PHP 8.3+)
}

echo Database::MYSQL;

// Magic constants
echo __LINE__;  // current line
echo __FILE__;  // full path
echo __DIR__;   // directory
echo __CLASS__;  // class name

String & Array Operators: String operators: . (concatenation), .= (append). Array operators: + (union, keeps left keys), == (same key/value pairs), === (same order and types), !=, !==, <> (inequality). Union + does not overwrite left with right keys.

<?php
// String operators
$greeting = 'Hello' . ' ' . 'World';
$greeting .= '!';
echo $greeting;  // Hello World!

// Array operators
$a = ['a' => 1, 'b' => 2];
$b = ['b' => 3, 'c' => 4];

$union = $a + $b;
print_r($union);  // ['a'=>1, 'b'=>2, 'c'=>4] (left wins)

// Array comparison
var_dump([1, 2] == [1, 2]);   // true
var_dump([1, 2] === [1, 2]);  // true
var_dump([1, 2] == [2, 1]);   // false

// instanceof operator
class User {}
$user = new User();
var_dump($user instanceof User);  // true
var_dump($user instanceof \Traversable);  // false
Arithmetic & Assignment: Standard arithmetic: + - * / % ** (PHP 5.6+). Assignment: =, +=, -=, *=, /=, %=, .= (string concat). Increment/decrement: ++$x, $x++, --$x, $x--. Integer division with intdiv(). Modulo on negatives follows dividend sign.

<?php
// Arithmetic
$a = 10 + 3;    // 13
$b = 10 - 3;    // 7
$c = 10 * 3;    // 30
$d = 10 / 3;    // 3.333
$e = 10 % 3;    // 1
$f = 2 ** 10;   // 1024

// Division variants
var_dump(intdiv(10, 3));    // int(3)
var_dump(fmod(10.5, 3));    // float(1.5)

// Assignment with operation
$x = 5;
$x += 3;  // 8
$x .= 'hello';  // '8hello' (string concat)

// Increment/decrement
$i = 0;
echo ++$i;  // 1 (pre-increment)
echo $i++;  // 1 (post-increment)
echo $i;    // 2
Comparison & Spaceship: Comparison operators: == (equal), === (identical), != (not equal), !== (not identical), < > <= >=. The spaceship operator <=> returns -1, 0, or 1. Useful for sorting callbacks usort(). Compare different types using PHP's type comparison table.

<?php
// Standard
var_dump(5 > 3);    // bool(true)
var_dump(5 <=> 3);  // int(1)
var_dump(3 <=> 3);  // int(0)
var_dump(1 <=> 3);  // int(-1)

// Sorting with spaceship
$items = ['cherry', 'Apple', 'banana'];
usort($items, fn($a, $b) => $a <=> $b);  // case-sensitive
usort($items, fn($a, $b) => strcasecmp($a, $b));  // case-insensitive

// String comparison
var_dump('apple' < 'banana');  // true
var_dump('5' < '12');          // true (string comparison, not numeric!)
var_dump('5' < 12);            // true (numeric comparison)

// Null coalescing (??)
$username = $_GET['user'] ?? 'Guest';

// Elvis operator (?:)
$name = $input ?: 'default';  //  if truthy else default
Logical & Bitwise: Logical: && (and), || (or), ! (not), and, or, xor. &&/|| have higher precedence than and/or. Short-circuit: && stops on false, || stops on true. Bitwise: & (and), | (or), ^ (xor), ~ (not), << (shift left), >> (shift right). Bitwise for flags/permissions.

<?php
// Logical — short-circuit
$result = true && false;   // false (evaluates both)
$result = false && risky();  // false (short-circuits, risky() not called)
$result = true || risky();   // true (short-circuits)

// Precedence
$result = true && false || true;  // true
$result = true and false || true; // true (and has lower precedence)

// Bitwise operations
$flags = 0b0011;  // 3
$mask  = 0b0101;  // 5
var_dump(decbin($flags & $mask));  // 0001
var_dump(decbin($flags | $mask));  // 0111
var_dump(decbin($flags ^ $mask));  // 0110
var_dump(decbin(~$flags));         // ...1100

// Practical: permissions
const READ = 0b100;   // 4
const WRITE = 0b010;  // 2
const EXEC = 0b001;   // 1
$perms = READ | WRITE;  // 6
if ($perms & READ) echo 'can read';  // yes

declare & Ticks: declare() sets execution directives for a block of code. Directives: strict_types (type coercion), encoding (script encoding), ticks (callback on N low-level statements). ticks are useful for profiling, progress tracking, and implementing signal-like behavior. declare(ticks=1) fires a tick handler every N statements.

<?php
// declare(strict_types=1) — enforces strict typing
// Must be first statement in file (before any other code)
declare(strict_types=1);

// Ticks — run function every N statements
function tickHandler(): void
{
    static $count = 0;
    $count++;
    // echo "Tick $count\n";
}

register_tick_function('tickHandler');

declare(ticks=1);

$x = 1;    // tick
$y = 2;    // tick
$z = $x + $y;  // tick

// Encoding directive (rarely used)
// declare(encoding='UTF-8');
goto & Labels: PHP supports goto operator for jumping to a named label. Labels defined with label:. goto must stay within the same file and scope — cannot jump into a function/loop. Use sparingly; goto can make code unreadable. Legitimate uses: breaking out of deeply nested structures or complex error recovery.

<?php
// Breaking out of nested loops
for ($i = 0; $i < 10; $i++) {
    for ($j = 0; $j < 10; $j++) {
        if ($i * $j > 50) {
            goto found;
        }
    }
}

echo "Not found\n";
exit;

found:
echo "Found at $i x $j = " . ($i * $j) . "\n";

// Cleanup pattern
$handle = fopen('file.txt', 'r');
if (!$handle) {
    goto cleanup;
}
// ... use handle

cleanup:
if (isset($handle)) fclose($handle);
// Consider try/finally instead
if/else/elseif: Standard conditional execution. elseif (one word) is the recommended form over else if (two words, requires braces). Use switch for many conditions on the same variable. Match (PHP 8+) is a stricter switch without loose comparison.

<?php
$score = 85;

if ($score >= 90) {
    echo 'A';
} elseif ($score >= 80) {
    echo 'B';
} else {
    echo 'C';
}

// Alternative syntax with :
if ($score >= 80):
    echo "Pass";
endif;
switch & match: switch compares loosely (==). Use break to prevent fall-through; default for no match. match (PHP 8+) compares strictly (===), returns a value, and doesn't require break. match throws UnhandledMatchError on no match.

<?php
$status = 404;

switch ($status) {
    case 200:
        echo 'OK';
        break;
    case 404:
        echo 'Not Found';
        break;
    default:
        echo 'Unknown';
}

// match (PHP 8+)
$result = match ($status) {
    200 => 'OK',
    404 => 'Not Found',
    500 => 'Server Error',
    default => 'Unknown',
};
echo $result;
for & foreach: for loops use counter (init; condition; increment). foreach is the preferred way to iterate arrays: foreach($arr as $value) or foreach($arr as $key => $value). Use break to exit, continue to skip iteration.

<?php
// for loop
for ($i = 0; $i < 5; $i++) {
    echo "Count: $i\n";
}

// foreach with array
$fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry'];
foreach ($fruits as $fruit) {
    echo $fruit;
}

// foreach with key => value
$ages = ['Alice' => 30, 'Bob' => 25];
foreach ($ages as $name => $age) {
    echo "$name is $age";
}
while & do-while: while runs before checking condition (may run 0 times). do-while runs at least once. Use with caution to avoid infinite loops. Common for reading data until exhausted.

<?php
$i = 0;
while ($i < 3) {
    echo "While: $i\n";
    $i++;
}

// do-while runs at least once
$j = 0;
do {
    echo "Do: $j\n";
    $j++;
} while ($j < 3);

// Reading file line by line
$handle = fopen("file.txt", "r");
while (($line = fgets($handle)) !== false) {
    echo $line;
}
fclose($handle);

Variable Scope: Variables defined outside functions are global — use global keyword to access them inside functions. Static variables persist between calls. Function parameters are local. The $GLOBALS superglobal provides access to all global variables.

<?php
$globalVar = 'outside';

function test() {
    global $globalVar;
    echo $globalVar;
    
    static $count = 0;
    $count++;
    echo $count;
}

test();  // outside, 1
test();  // outside, 2

// Via $GLOBALS
function test2() {
    echo $GLOBALS['globalVar'];
}
Variable Functions & Callbacks: If a variable name has parentheses appended, PHP looks for a function with that name. call_user_func() and call_user_func_array() call callbacks. Useful for dynamic dispatch and event handling.

<?php
function hello() { echo "Hello!"; }
function bye() { echo "Bye!"; }

$func = 'hello';
$func();  // calls hello()

$func = 'bye';
$func();  // calls bye()

// With parameters
function add(int $a, int $b): int { return $a + $b; }
call_user_func('add', 3, 4);
call_user_func_array('add', [3, 4]);
Arrow Functions Deep: Arrow functions (PHP 7.4+) provide concise anonymous function syntax: fn($x) => expr. They implicitly capture outer-scope variables by value (no use() needed). Cannot use by-reference binding. Single expression only (no multi-statement). Nestable. Useful for array_map/filter callbacks and short closures.

<?php
// Arrow function
$multiply = fn($a, $b) => $a * $b;
echo $multiply(3, 4);  // 12

// Implicit by-value capture
$factor = 2;
$doubled = array_map(fn($n) => $n * $factor, [1, 2, 3]);
// [2, 4, 6]

// Compare with anonymous function
$anonymous = function($n) use ($factor) { return $n * $factor; };

// Nested arrow function
$process = fn($items) => array_map(fn($i) => $i * 2, $items);
print_r($process([1, 2, 3]));  // [2, 4, 6]

// Callbacks
usort($items, fn($a, $b) => $a->sortKey <=> $b->sortKey);

// Arrow functions as closures
$counter = 0;
$increment = fn() => $counter + 1;  // reads $counter, can't modify it
// Must use reference: $increment = function() use (&$counter) { return ++$counter; };
Defining Functions: Functions are defined with the function keyword. They can have typed parameters and return types (PHP 7+). Default parameter values are supported. Use return to return a value; functions without return return null.

<?php
function greet(string $name): string {
    return "Hello, $name!";
}

echo greet('Alice');

// Default parameters
function multiply(int $a, int $b = 2): int {
    return $a * $b;
}

echo multiply(5);     // 10
echo multiply(5, 3);  // 15
Anonymous Functions & Closures: Anonymous functions (closures) can be assigned to variables or passed as arguments. Use function ($arg) use ($var) { ... } to import variables from the outer scope. Arrow functions (PHP 7.4+) provide shorter syntax with fn($arg) => expr.

<?php
// Anonymous function
$greet = function(string $name): string {
    return "Hello, $name!";
};
echo $greet('Alice');

// Closure with use
$prefix = "User: ";
$formatName = function(string $name) use ($prefix): string {
    return $prefix . $name;
};

// Arrow function (PHP 7.4+)
$multiply = fn($a, $b) => $a * $b;
echo $multiply(3, 4);  // 12

// As callback
$numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4];
$squared = array_map(fn($n) => $n * $n, $numbers);
Variadic Params & Spread: Variadic parameters capture variable arguments into an array. Prefix last param with ...$args. The spread operator (...) unpacks arrays into function arguments (PHP 5.6+). Named arguments (PHP 8+) can be combined with variadic. Use variadic for flexible APIs, middleware, and logging.

<?php
// Variadic parameter
function sum(int ...$numbers): int {
    return array_sum($numbers);
}

echo sum(1, 2, 3, 4);  // 10

// Variadic with named params
function log(string $level, string ...$messages): void {
    foreach ($messages as $msg) {
        echo "[$level] $msg\n";
    }
}

log('INFO', 'Started', 'Processing', 'Done');

// Spread operator in call
$args = [1, 2, 3, 4];
echo sum(...$args);  // 10

// Merge arrays with spread (PHP 7.4+)
$a = [1, 2];
$b = [3, 4];
$merged = [...$a, ...$b];  // [1, 2, 3, 4]

// Spread in named arguments (PHP 8.1+)
function create(string $name, int $age, string $country): void {}
$params = ['name' => 'Alice', 'age' => 30, 'country' => 'US'];
create(...$params);
Callable & Invocable: Callable is a pseudo-type accepted by functions like array_map, usort. Callables can be: string function name, array [class/object, method], Closure, or invocable object (with __invoke). Use is_callable() to check. call_user_func() and call_user_func_array() invoke callables dynamically.

<?php
// Callable types
$callable1 = 'strtoupper';           // string function name
$callable2 = ['User', 'find'];        // static method
$callable3 = [$user, 'getName'];      // instance method
$callable4 = function($x) { return $x; };  // closure

// Invocable object
class Adder {
    public function __invoke(int $a, int $b): int {
        return $a + $b;
    }
}

$adder = new Adder();
echo $adder(3, 4);  // 7 (object invoked as function)

// Check callable
if (is_callable($callable1)) {
    echo array_map($callable1, ['a', 'b']);  // ['A', 'B']
}

// Using callable type hint
function transform(array $items, callable $callback): array {
    return array_map($callback, $items);
}
Type Declarations: PHP 7+ supports scalar type declarations: int, float, string, bool, void, iterable, mixed (PHP 8+), never (PHP 8.1+). Nullable types use ? prefix (e.g., ?string). Union types (PHP 8+) use | (e.g., int|string). Strict mode enabled with declare(strict_types=1).

<?php
declare(strict_types=1);

function add(int $a, int $b): int {
    return $a + $b;
}

// Nullable type
function find(?string $id): ?array {
    if ($id === null) return null;
    return ['id' => $id];
}

// Union type (PHP 8+)
function format(int|string $value): string {
    return (string) $value;
}

String Functions: PHP has a vast standard library of string functions. strlen(), substr(), str_replace(), strpos(), strtolower(), strtoupper(), trim(), explode(), implode(), str_repeat(), str_pad(). PHP 8 added: str_contains(), str_starts_with(), str_ends_with(). Most functions are multi-byte safe with mb_* variants.

<?php
$text = "Hello, World!";

echo strlen($text);              // 13
echo substr($text, 7, 5);       // 'World'
echo str_replace('World', 'PHP', $text);  // 'Hello, PHP!'
echo strpos($text, 'World');    // 7
echo strtolower($text);         // 'hello, world!'
echo trim('  hello  ');         // 'hello'

// PHP 8+
var_dump(str_contains($text, 'World'));    // true
var_dump(str_starts_with($text, 'Hello')); // true

// Split and join
$parts = explode(', ', $text);  // ['Hello', 'World!']
echo implode(' | ', $parts);   // 'Hello | World!'

// Padding
str_pad('PHP', 10, '-', STR_PAD_BOTH);  // '---PHP----'
Multi-byte Strings: Standard PHP string functions assume single-byte characters. Use mb_* (multi-byte) functions for UTF-8 and other encodings: mb_strlen(), mb_substr(), mb_strpos(), mb_strtolower(), etc. Enable mbstring extension. Always use mb_* for user input and international text. Check encoding with mb_detect_encoding().

<?php
// Multi-byte strings (UTF-8)
$text = 'Hëllö Wörld';

echo strlen($text);    // 15 (byte count)
echo mb_strlen($text); // 11 (character count)

echo substr($text, 0, 3);    // 'Hë' (may corrupt if multi-byte)
echo mb_substr($text, 0, 3); // 'Hël'

$html = 'über
';
echo strip_tags($html);       // OK: 'über'
echo mb_strtolower($text);    // 'hëllö wörld'

// Encoding detection
$enc = mb_detect_encoding($text, ['UTF-8', 'ISO-8859-1']);
echo $enc;  // 'UTF-8'

// Convert encoding
$latin = mb_convert_encoding($text, 'ISO-8859-1', 'UTF-8');

// Always use mb_ for user input
mb_regex_encoding('UTF-8');
sprintf & printf: sprintf() returns a formatted string, printf() outputs it. Format specifiers: %s (string), %d (int), %f (float), %x (hex), %c (char). Width and precision: %10s (right-align width 10), %-10s (left-align), %.2f (2 decimal places), %'_-10s (pad with _). vsprintf() for array arguments.

<?php
$name = 'Alice';
$age = 30;

// Basic formatting
$msg = sprintf('Name: %s, Age: %d', $name, $age);
echo $msg;  // 'Name: Alice, Age: 30'

// Width and alignment
echo sprintf("|%10s|", 'right');   // '|     right|'
echo sprintf("|%-10s|", 'left');    // '|left     |'
echo sprintf("|%'_-10s|", 'pad');   // '|_______pad|'

// Number formatting
printf('Pi: %.2f', M_PI);        // 'Pi: 3.14'

printf('%,d', 1234567);          // '1,234,567'

// Argument swapping (PHP 4.0.6+)
echo sprintf('%2$s is %1$d years old', 30, 'Alice');
// 'Alice is 30 years old'

<?php
$fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry'];
echo $fruits[0];  // apple

$fruits[] = 'date';           // append
array_push($fruits, 'elderberry');
$last = array_pop($fruits);
$first = array_shift($fruits);
array_unshift($fruits, 'apricot');

echo count($fruits);
print_r($fruits);
Associative Arrays: Associative arrays use string keys. Useful for key-value mappings and structured data. Access with $arr['key'] or $arr[$key]. Check key existence with isset() or array_key_exists(). Merge arrays with array_merge().

<?php
$user = [
    'name' => 'Alice',
    'age' => 30,
    'email' => 'alice@example.com'
];

echo $user['name'];

// Check key
if (isset($user['email'])) {
    echo "Email exists";
}

// Merge
$defaults = ['role' => 'user', 'active' => true];
$user = array_merge($defaults, $user);

// Iterate
foreach ($user as $key => $value) {
    echo "$key: $value\n";
}
Multidimensional Arrays: Arrays can contain other arrays for nested data structures. Access with multiple indices ($arr[0]['name']). Useful for representing complex data like tables, matrices, or nested records.
Array Functions: PHP has a rich set of array functions: array_map (transform), array_filter (filter), array_reduce (aggregate), array_merge (combine), array_diff (difference), array_intersect (common), array_keys (get keys), array_values (get values), sort functions (sort, rsort, asort, ksort, usort).

<?php
$numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];

// Transform
$squared = array_map(fn($n) => $n * $n, $numbers);

// Filter
$even = array_filter($numbers, fn($n) => $n % 2 === 0);

// Reduce
$sum = array_reduce($numbers, fn($carry, $n) => $carry + $n, 0);

// Sort
$fruits = ['cherry', 'apple', 'banana'];
sort($fruits);              // ascending
rsort($fruits);             // descending
asort($fruits);             // maintain keys
ksort($fruits);             // sort by keys
Array Sorting: PHP provides multiple sort functions: sort (value ascending), rsort (descending), asort (value ascending, keep keys), ksort (key ascending), arsort/ krsort (reverse). usort for custom comparison. natcasesort for natural order. array_multisort for multi-dimensional sorting. SORT_REGULAR, SORT_NUMERIC, SORT_STRING flags control comparison type.

<?php
$fruits = ['cherry', 'Apple', 'banana'];

sort($fruits);           // ['Apple', 'banana', 'cherry'] (case-sensitive)

// Natural sort (case-insensitive)
natsort($fruits);        // preserves keys
// natcasesort() — case-insensitive version

// Custom sort with spaceship
usort($fruits, fn($a, $b) => $a <=> $b);

// Sort by key
$ages = ['Alice' => 30, 'Bob' => 25, 'Charlie' => 35];
ksort($ages);  // Alice, Bob, Charlie (alphabetical by name)
asort($ages);  // Bob(25), Alice(30), Charlie(35) (by age)

// Multi-dimensional sort
$data = [
    ['name' => 'Alice', 'age' => 30],
    ['name' => 'Bob', 'age' => 25],
];
usort($data, fn($a, $b) => $a['age'] <=> $b['age']);

// Multiple criteria
usort($data, fn($a, $b) => [$a['age'], $a['name']] <=> [$b['age'], $b['name']]);
Array Destructuring: Array destructuring extracts values into variables. Symmetric array destructuring with [$a, $b] = $array (PHP 7.1+). Also works with foreach. Supports nested destructuring, skipping elements, and keyed destructuring (PHP 7.1+). list() is the older syntax with same functionality. Useful for swapping variables, unpacking tuples, and clean extraction.

<?php
// Basic destructuring
[$a, $b] = [1, 2];
echo $a;  // 1
echo $b;  // 2

// Skip elements
[$first, , $third] = [1, 2, 3];
echo $first;  // 1
echo $third;  // 3

// Nested destructuring
$data = [[1, 2], [3, 4]];
foreach ($data as [$x, $y]) {
    echo "($x, $y) ";  // (1, 2) (3, 4)
}

// Keyed destructuring (PHP 7.1+)
['name' => $name, 'age' => $age] = ['name' => 'Alice', 'age' => 30];
echo $name;  // Alice

// Variable swapping
[$a, $b] = [$b, $a];

// In foreach
$users = [
    ['id' => 1, 'name' => 'Alice'],
    ['id' => 2, 'name' => 'Bob'],
];
foreach ($users as ['id' => $id, 'name' => $name]) {
    echo "$id: $name\n";
}
SPL Data Structures: SPL (Standard PHP Library) provides built-in data structures: SplStack, SplQueue, SplHeap, SplPriorityQueue, SplFixedArray, SplObjectStorage. These are more memory-efficient than plain arrays for specific use cases.

<?php
// Stack (LIFO)
$stack = new SplStack();
$stack->push('first');
$stack->push('second');
echo $stack->pop();  // second

// Queue (FIFO)
$queue = new SplQueue();
$queue->enqueue('first');
$queue->enqueue('second');
echo $queue->dequeue();  // first

// Fixed array (better memory)
$fixed = new SplFixedArray(3);
$fixed[0] = 'a';
$fixed[1] = 'b';

Magic Methods: PHP magic methods (__construct, __destruct, __call, __get, __set, __toString, __invoke, __clone, __debugInfo) intercept operations on objects. __get/__set handle undefined property access. __call/__callStatic handle undefined method calls. __toString specifies string representation. __invoke makes objects callable. Use sparingly — they make code harder to reason about.

<?php
class Magic
{
    private array $data = [];

    // Property overloading
    public function __get(string $name): mixed
    {
        return $this->data[$name] ?? null;
    }

    public function __set(string $name, mixed $value): void
    {
        $this->data[$name] = $value;
    }

    public function __isset(string $name): bool
    {
        return isset($this->data[$name]);
    }

    // Method overloading
    public function __call(string $name, array $args): mixed
    {
        return "Called $name with " . json_encode($args);
    }

    public static function __callStatic(string $name, array $args): mixed
    {
        return "Static call: $name";
    }

    // String conversion
    public function __toString(): string
    {
        return json_encode($this->data);
    }

    // Debug info
    public function __debugInfo(): array
    {
        return ['data' => $this->data];
    }
}

$obj = new Magic();
$obj->name = 'Alice';  // __set
echo $obj->name;        // __get
$obj->unknownMethod();  // __call
Static Methods & Properties: Static members belong to the class, not instances. Accessed with :: (Scope Resolution Operator). self:: refers to the current class, static:: refers to the called class (late static binding). parent:: accesses parent class.

<?php
class Database {
    private static ?Database $instance = null;
    
    public static function getInstance(): self {
        if (self::$instance === null) {
            self::$instance = new self();
        }
        return self::$instance;
    }
    
    private function __construct() {}
    
    public static function connect(): string {
        return "Connected";
    }
}

$db = Database::getInstance();
echo Database::connect();
Abstract Classes & Late Static Binding: Abstract classes (declared abstract) define base functionality with abstract methods that subclasses must implement. Late Static Binding (LSB) uses static:: instead of self:: to reference the called class at runtime. static:: binds to the class that was actually called, not where the method is defined. Use for factory methods and polymorphic behavior.

<?php
abstract class Database
{
    abstract protected function connect(): void;
    
    public function query(string $sql): array
    {
        $this->connect();
        return [];  // fetched results
    }
    
    // Factory method with LSB
    public static function create(): static
    {
        return new static();
    }
}

class MySQL extends Database
{
    protected function connect(): void
    {
        echo "Connecting to MySQL\n";
    }
}

class PostgreSQL extends Database
{
    protected function connect(): void
    {
        echo "Connecting to PostgreSQL\n";
    }
}

// Late Static Binding
$db = MySQL::create();   // returns MySQL instance
$db = PostgreSQL::create();  // returns PostgreSQL instance

// self:: vs static::
class Base {
    public static function who(): string { return 'Base'; }
    public static function testSelf(): string { return self::who(); }
    public static function testStatic(): string { return static::who(); }
}

class Child extends Base {
    public static function who(): string { return 'Child'; }
}

echo Child::testSelf();    // 'Base' (self binds to Base)
echo Child::testStatic();  // 'Child' (static binds to Child)
Classes & Objects: Classes define blueprints for objects. new creates instances. $this refers to the current instance. Properties and methods can be public, protected, or private. Constructor __construct() initializes properties. Type declarations work on properties (PHP 7.4+) and promoted properties (PHP 8+).

<?php
class User {
    public function __construct(
        private string $name,
        private int $age
    ) {}
    
    public function greet(): string {
        return "Hello, I'm {$this->name}";
    }
    
    public function getName(): string {
        return $this->name;
    }
}

$user = new User('Alice', 30);
echo $user->greet();
echo $user->getName();
Inheritance: extends creates a child class that inherits parent methods and properties. Use parent:: to call parent methods. Override methods by redefining them. final keyword prevents overriding. abstract classes define base functionality with abstract methods.

<?php
class Animal {
    public function __construct(protected string $name) {}
    
    public function speak(): string {
        return "$this->name makes a sound";
    }
}

class Dog extends Animal {
    public function speak(): string {
        return "$this->name barks";
    }
}

$dog = new Dog('Buddy');
echo $dog->speak();

// Abstract class
abstract class Shape {
    abstract public function area(): float;
}

class Circle extends Shape {
    public function __construct(private float $radius) {}
    public function area(): float {
        return pi() * $this->radius ** 2;
    }
}
Interfaces & Traits: Interfaces define contracts with method signatures. A class can implement multiple interfaces. Traits enable horizontal code reuse — they're like partial classes. Use traits with the use keyword inside a class.

<?php
interface Logger {
    public function log(string $message): void;
}

interface Notifier {
    public function send(string $to, string $message): void;
}

trait Timestampable {
    public function getTimestamp(): string {
        return date('Y-m-d H:i:s');
    }
}

class AppLogger implements Logger, Notifier {
    use Timestampable;
    
    public function log(string $message): void {
        echo "[{$this->getTimestamp()}] $message";
    }
    
    public function send(string $to, string $message): void {
        mail($to, "Alert", $message);
    }
}
Namespaces: Namespaces organize code and prevent naming conflicts. Declare with namespace at file top. Import with use keyword. Aliases with use ... as .... Fully qualified names start with \ (global namespace). Follow PSR-4 for autoloading.

<?php
namespace App\Models;

class User {
    // ...
}

// Another file
namespace App\Controllers;

use App\Models\User;
use App\Helpers\Format as Fmt;

$user = new User();
Fmt::formatText('hello');
Anonymous Classes: PHP 7.0+ supports anonymous classes created on-the-fly with new class { ... }. They can extend other classes, implement interfaces, and use traits. Useful for one-off objects, mocks in tests, and small adapters. Anonymous classes can be passed to functions and closures. They get a runtime-generated name.

<?php
// Basic anonymous class
$logger = new class {
    public function log(string $msg): void
    {
        echo "Log: $msg\n";
    }
};

$logger->log('Hello');  // Log: Hello

// With constructor and interface
$cache = new class('redis') implements CacheInterface {
    private string $driver;
    
    public function __construct(string $driver)
    {
        $this->driver = $driver;
    }

// Testing mock
$service = new class extends BaseService {

$wrapper = new class($dependency) {

File Info & Directories: File functions: basename(), dirname(), pathinfo(), filesize(), filemtime(), filetype(). Directory functions: mkdir(), rmdir(), scandir(), glob(). Recursive directory iteration with RecursiveDirectoryIterator.

<?php
// File info
$path = '/path/to/file.txt';
echo basename($path);      // file.txt
echo dirname($path);       // /path/to
echo filesize('file.txt');
echo filemtime('file.txt');

// Directory operations
mkdir('newdir', 0755, true);  // recursive
$files = scandir('.');

// Recursive directory iterator
$it = new RecursiveIteratorIterator(
    new RecursiveDirectoryIterator('.')
);

    if ($file->isFile()) {
        echo $file->getPathname() . "\n";
    }
}
CSV & JSON Processing: PHP provides built-in functions for CSV and JSON. fgetcsv()/fputcsv() for CSV I/O. json_encode()/json_decode() for JSON. JSON flags: JSON_PRETTY_PRINT, JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR (PHP 7.3+), JSON_FORCE_OBJECT. CSV flags for delimiters and enclosure. Handle large files with streaming (fgetcsv in loop).

<?php
// CSV reading
$handle = fopen('data.csv', 'r');
$headers = fgetcsv($handle);  // first row as headers
$rows = [];
while (($row = fgetcsv($handle)) !== false) {
    $rows[] = array_combine($headers, $row);
}
fclose($handle);

// CSV writing
$handle = fopen('output.csv', 'w');
fputcsv($handle, ['name', 'age', 'city']);
fputcsv($handle, ['Alice', 30, 'NYC']);
fputcsv($handle, ['Bob', 25, 'SF']);
fclose($handle);

// JSON
$data = ['name' => 'Alice', 'age' => 30, 'tags' => ['php', 'web']];

$json = json_encode($data, JSON_PRETTY_PRINT | JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR);
file_put_contents('data.json', $json);

$decoded = json_decode(file_get_contents('data.json'), true);
echo $decoded['name'];  // Alice

// Error handling
$result = json_decode('{invalid}', true);
if (json_last_error() !== JSON_ERROR_NONE) {
    echo 'JSON error: ' . json_last_error_msg();
}
File Uploads: Files are uploaded via POST forms with enctype="multipart/form-data". Access via $_FILES superglobal. Use move_uploaded_file() to store. Validate file type, size, and errors. Beware of security: validate extensions, limit size, scan for malware.

<?php
// HTML form: <form method="POST" enctype="multipart/form-data">
// <input type="file" name="document">

if ($_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD'] === 'POST') {
    $file = $_FILES['document'];
    
    if ($file['error'] === UPLOAD_ERR_OK) {
        $ext = pathinfo($file['name'], PATHINFO_EXTENSION);
        $allowed = ['pdf', 'doc', 'txt'];
        
        if (in_array($ext, $allowed)) {
            $dest = 'uploads/' . uniqid() . '.' . $ext;
            move_uploaded_file($file['tmp_name'], $dest);
            echo "Uploaded to $dest";
        }
    }
}
Reading Files: file_get_contents() reads entire file as string. file() reads into array by lines. fopen() with fread()/fgets() provides streaming access. feof() checks end-of-file. Always close with fclose(). Use file_exists() and is_readable() to check first.

<?php
// Simple read
$content = file_get_contents('file.txt');

// Read into array
$lines = file('file.txt');

// Streaming read
$handle = fopen('file.txt', 'r');
if ($handle) {
    while (($line = fgets($handle)) !== false) {
        echo $line;
    }
    fclose($handle);
}

// Check before reading
if (file_exists('file.txt') && is_readable('file.txt')) {
    $content = file_get_contents('file.txt');
}
Writing Files: file_put_contents() writes string to file (replaces). Use FILE_APPEND flag to append. fopen() with w (write), a (append), x (create exclusive) modes. flock() for file locking. fwrite() for streaming writes.

<?php
// Simple write
file_put_contents('file.txt', 'Hello World');

// Append
file_put_contents('file.txt', "\nNew line", FILE_APPEND);

// With stream
$handle = fopen('file.txt', 'w');
flock($handle, LOCK_EX);
fwrite($handle, "Line 1\n");
fwrite($handle, "Line 2\n");
flock($handle, LOCK_UN);
fclose($handle);

// Create only if not exists
file_put_contents('new.txt', 'content', LOCK_EX);

<?php
// URL: /page.php?name=Alice&age=30

<?php
$email = $_POST['email'] ?? '';

}

XSS Prevention & Output Escaping: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) is prevented by escaping output. Use htmlspecialchars() with ENT_QUOTES and UTF-8 for HTML context. For URLs: urlencode(). For JS: json_encode() (safe). For CSS/HTML attributes: escape appropriately per context. Content Security Policy (CSP) headers add a defense layer. Never trust user input — escape on output, not input.

<?php
// HTML escaped output
$userInput = "<script>alert('xss')</script>";
echo htmlspecialchars($userInput, ENT_QUOTES | ENT_SUBSTITUTE, 'UTF-8');
// <script>alert('xss')</script>

// URL context
$url = "https://example.com?q=" . urlencode($userInput);

// JavaScript context (use json_encode for safety)
$jsSafe = json_encode($userInput, JSON_HEX_TAG | JSON_HEX_AMP);
echo "<script>var name = $jsSafe;</script>";

// HTML attribute
$attrValue = htmlspecialchars($userInput, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8');
echo "<input value='$attrValue'>";

// CSP header
header("Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'");

// Template engines (Twig, Blade) auto-escape
// {{ user_input }} is escaped by default in Twig

$stmt->execute([18]);
$users = $stmt->fetchAll();

$stmt = $pdo->prepare('DELETE FROM users WHERE id = ?');

DateTime Class: The DateTime class provides OOP date/time handling. Create with new DateTime() or new DateTime('2026-01-15'). Format with format('Y-m-d H:i:s'). Modify with modify('+1 day'). Diff returns DateInterval. Timezone handling with setTimezone(). Immutable version: DateTimeImmutable (recommended).

<?php
$now = new DateTime();
echo $now->format('Y-m-d H:i:s');

// Create from string
$date = new DateTime('2026-01-15 10:30:00');
echo $date->format('Y-m-d');  // 2026-01-15

// Modify (mutable)
$date->modify('+1 week');
echo $date->format('Y-m-d');

// DateTimeImmutable (returns new instance)
$immutable = new DateTimeImmutable('2026-01-01');
$nextWeek = $immutable->modify('+1 week');
echo $immutable->format('Y-m-d');  // still 2026-01-01
echo $nextWeek->format('Y-m-d');   // 2026-01-08

// Diff
$future = new DateTime('2027-01-01');
$interval = $now->diff($future);
echo $interval->days;  // total days

// Timezone
$utc = new DateTime('now', new DateTimeZone('UTC'));
$nyc = (clone $utc)->setTimezone(new DateTimeZone('America/New_York'));

Create intervals with new DateInterval('P1M') or DateInterval::createFromDateString. Use for recurring events, schedules, and date ranges.

<?php
// Create interval
$weekly = new DateInterval('P1W');  // 1 week
$custom = DateInterval::createFromDateString('3 months + 2 days');

// Format interval
$interval = $now->diff($future);
echo $interval->format('%y years, %m months, %d days');

// DatePeriod (iteration)
$start = new DateTime('2026-01-01');
$end = new DateTime('2026-03-01');
$interval = new DateInterval('P2W');

$period = new DatePeriod($start, $interval, $end);
foreach ($period as $date) {
    echo $date->format('Y-m-d') . "\n";
}
// 2026-01-01, 2026-01-15, 2026-01-29, 2026-02-12, 2026-02-26

// Recurring events
echo (new DateTime('2026-01-31'))->modify('+1 month')->format('Y-m-d');
// 2026-03-03 (PHP handles variable month lengths)

Supports: 'now', 'tomorrow', 'next Monday', '+2 weeks', 'first day of next month', 'last day of December 2026'. Returns int (timestamp) or false. Combine with date() for formatting. Beware of ambiguous dates (e.g., '01/02/03' is m/d/y in US).

<?php
// Relative dates
echo date('Y-m-d', strtotime('now'));
echo date('Y-m-d', strtotime('tomorrow'));
echo date('Y-m-d', strtotime('next Monday'));
echo date('Y-m-d', strtotime('+2 weeks'));
echo date('Y-m-d', strtotime('last day of next month'));
echo date('Y-m-d', strtotime('first day of January 2027'));

// strtotime with base timestamp (PHP 5.3+)
$base = strtotime('2026-06-01');
echo date('Y-m-d', strtotime('+3 weeks', $base));

// Check for parse failure
$ts = strtotime('invalid date');
if ($ts === false) {

$dt = new DateTime('@' . strtotime('next Monday'));
echo $dt->format('c');

// Microseconds

Enums (PHP 8.1): Enums (PHP 8.1+) define a set of named constants. Pure enums (case only) and backed enums (with scalar value: int or string). Methods and static methods are supported. match works perfectly with enums. Enum values are objects (not just constants). Use for status codes, options, and finite sets of values.

<?php
// Pure enum
enum Status
{
    case Active;
    case Inactive;
    case Archived;
}

// Backed enum (int or string)
enum HttpStatus: int
{
    case OK = 200;
    case NotFound = 404;
    case ServerError = 500;
}

// Usage
$status = Status::Active;

// Match with enum
function describe(Status $s): string
{
    return match ($s) {
        Status::Active => 'Active and visible',
        Status::Inactive => 'Hidden from users',
        Status::Archived => 'Read-only archive',
    };
}

// Backed value
echo HttpStatus::NotFound->value;  // 404
$parsed = HttpStatus::from(404);   // HttpStatus::NotFound
$parsed = HttpStatus::tryFrom(999); // null

// Enum methods
enum Color
{
    case Red;
    case Green;
    case Blue;

    public function hex(): string
    {
        return match ($this) {
            self::Red => '#FF0000',
            self::Green => '#00FF00',
            self::Blue => '#0000FF',
        };
    }
}
Fibers (PHP 8.1): Fibers are lightweight cooperative concurrency primitives (PHP 8.1+). Unlike threads, fibers voluntarily yield control via Fiber::suspend(). The parent resumes with Fiber::resume(). Fibers enable async/await patterns without callback nesting. Used internally by async frameworks (Amp, ReactPHP) for non-blocking I/O.

<?php
// Basic fiber
$fiber = new Fiber(function (): void {
    $value = Fiber::suspend('first suspend');
    echo "Resumed with: $value\n";
    Fiber::suspend('second suspend');
    return 'done';
});

// Start fiber
echo $fiber->start();  // 'first suspend'

// Resume with value
echo $fiber->resume('hello');  // 'second suspend'

// Get return value
echo $fiber->getReturn();  // 'done'

// Practical: non-blocking I/O pattern
$fiber = new Fiber(function () use ($httpClient): void {
    $response = $httpClient->request('https://api.example.com');
    $data = Fiber::suspend($response);  // yield while waiting
    // process $data
});

$response = $fiber->start();
// Do other work while HTTP request completes...
$data = $response->getBody();
$fiber->resume($data);

Shutdown & Error Handler Functions: register_shutdown_function() registers a callback that runs after script completion (or fatal error). set_error_handler() catches non-fatal errors. set_exception_handler() catches uncaught exceptions. Error types: E_ERROR (fatal), E_WARNING, E_NOTICE, E_USER_*, E_STRICT. Use error_get_last() to check the last error. These allow graceful degradation and logging.

<?php
// Global exception handler
set_exception_handler(function (\Throwable $e): void {
    error_log("Uncaught: " . $e->__toString());
    http_response_code(500);
    if (ini_get('display_errors')) {
        echo "Error: " . $e->getMessage();
    } else {
        echo "Internal server error";
    }
});

// Shutdown function (runs even on fatal)
register_shutdown_function(function (): void {
    $error = error_get_last();
    if ($error !== null && $error['type'] === E_ERROR) {
        error_log("Fatal: {$error['message']}");
    }
});

// Custom error handler
set_error_handler(function(int $severity, string $msg, string $file, int $line): bool {
    if (!(error_reporting() & $severity)) {
        return false;  // @ suppressed
    }
    throw new ErrorException($msg, 0, $severity, $file, $line);
});

// Trigger all error types
trigger_error('User notice', E_USER_NOTICE);
trigger_error('User warning', E_USER_WARNING);
Multiple Catch & Finally: PHP supports multiple catch blocks (one per exception type) and a finally block that always executes. Catch ordering matters — put specific exceptions before general ones. PHP 8.0+ supports catch without a variable (catch (Exception)). Multi-catch (same handler) uses pipe: catch (A|B $e). finally runs after try or catch for cleanup.

<?php
try {
    $data = processInput($input);
    $result = $db->save($data);
    $email->send($result);
} catch (ValidationException $e) {
    // Specific first
    http_response_code(422);
    echo json_encode(['error' => $e->getMessage()]);
} catch (DatabaseException $e) {
    // Different handling
    error_log($e->getMessage());
    http_response_code(500);
    echo 'Database error';
} catch (Exception $e) {
    // Catch-all (must be last)
    http_response_code(500);
    echo 'Unexpected error';
} finally {
    // Always runs (cleanup)
    $db->close();
    $logger->endRequest();
}

// Multi-catch (PHP 8.0+)
try {
    // ...
} catch (AException | BException $e) {
    // Same handler for both
}

// Catch without variable (PHP 8.0+)
try {
    // ...
} catch (RuntimeException) {
    echo "Runtime error occurred";
}

        throw new Exception('File not found');

} catch (Exception $e) {

    echo 'File: ' . $e->getFile();

SQL Injection Prevention: SQL injection is prevented by using prepared statements (always) and never concatenating user input into SQL. PDO and MySQLi both support prepared statements. Use bound parameters — they separate SQL logic from data. Additional layers: input validation, least-privilege database users, and escaping as defense-in-depth only.

<?php
// VULNERABLE — never do this:
// $sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $_GET[id]";

// SAFE — prepared statements
$pdo = new PDO('mysql:host=localhost;dbname=test', 'user', 'pass', [
    PDO::ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES => false,
]);

$stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = :email AND active = :active');
$stmt->execute(['email' => $_POST['email'], 'active' => true]);

// SAFE — with positional placeholders
$stmt = $pdo->prepare('INSERT INTO users (name, email) VALUES (?, ?)');
$stmt->execute([$_POST['name'], $_POST['email']]);

// Even for LIKE, use placeholders
$stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT * FROM users WHERE name LIKE ?');
$stmt->execute(['%' . $_GET['q'] . '%']);

Session security: use secure cookies (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite), regenerate session ID after login, set session timeout, use HTTPS. Content Security Policy (CSP) headers add another layer.

<?php
session_start();

// Generate CSRF token
if (empty($_SESSION['csrf_token'])) {
    $_SESSION['csrf_token'] = bin2hex(random_bytes(32));
}

// In form: <input type="hidden" name="csrf_token" value="<?= $_SESSION['csrf_token'] ?>">

// Validate on POST
if ($_POST['csrf_token'] !== $_SESSION['csrf_token']) {
    die('Invalid CSRF token');
}

// Session security settings
ini_set('session.cookie_httponly', '1');
ini_set('session.cookie_secure', '1');
ini_set('session.cookie_samesite', 'Lax');
ini_set('session.gc_maxlifetime', '3600');
ini_set('session.use_strict_mode', '1');

// Regenerate after login
session_regenerate_id(true);

// CSP header
header("Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'");
OPcache & Caching: OPcache improves performance by storing compiled PHP bytecode in shared memory, eliminating recompilation on each request. Enable in php.ini: opcache.enable=1, opcache.memory_consumption=128. File-based caching with file_put_contents/serialize or APCu for user data. Redis/Memcached for distributed caching. <?php
// php.ini OPcache settings
// opcache.enable=1
// opcache.memory_consumption=256
// opcache.max_accelerated_files=20000
// opcache.validate_timestamps=0  (production)

// Simple file cache
function cache_get(string $key): mixed
{
    $path = '/tmp/cache/' . md5($key);
    if (!file_exists($path)) return null;
    $data = file_get_contents($path);
    $entry = unserialize($data);
    return $entry['expires'] > time() ? $entry['data'] : null;
}

function cache_set(string $key, mixed $value, int $ttl = 3600): void
{
    $path = '/tmp/cache/' . md5($key);
    file_put_contents($path, serialize([
        'data' => $value,
        'expires' => time() + $ttl,
    ]));
}
